title: Vilasa 3. The Interruption of Srinivasa's Studies
html:
The author's address on the cause of his writing; Srinivasa's childhood — the first rice and the sacred thread; the break in his studies and the boy's grief; his teacher Dhananjaya admits that the pupil has surpassed him; Sarasvati, by Chaitanya's command, bestows all learning on Srinivasa

1Glory, glory to Sri Chaitanya Acharya, glory, glory!
Glory, glory to Lakshmipriya of compassionate heart!

2Glory, glory to the listeners — listen with care,
you whose life's treasure is the pastimes of Radha and Krishna's prema.

3Of one shortcoming of mine I will write once:1
at the feet of Krishna's devotees I bow.

4I have not studied, and there is not a trace of bhakti in me;
yet I write by the command of the Ocean of compassion:

5"All my devotees who wander upon the earth
descended along with me and bear the same virtues.

6Some have described the pastimes of Radha and Krishna,
others have revealed scriptures about Gaura's pastimes.

7Whoever writes of the virtues of Krishna's devotees,
to him I show mercy with a joyful heart.

8After my departure there will be prema upon the earth;
I bid you write and describe their virtues.

9Srinivasa and Narottama are the two Mahashayas;
write of the virtues of these two abundantly.

10Write of the virtues of both and of their way of bhajana —
how the earth spread prema in their form."

11I have never known a speck of the gift of description;
yet I write by the strength of the command of the two Lords.

12Sri Jahnava and Virachandra, at whose feet my hope rests —
from them came the command to reveal these virtues.

13Srinivasa is my breath, Narottama my life;
with care I write of the virtues of these two.

14By that command I write whatever words come to my mind;
O Vaishnava Gosanis, do not count it against me in any way.

15For six months the Acharya did not go out anywhere;
seeing his son's power, he remained at peace.

16Both rejoiced as they looked on their son's face,
and raised their son with happy hearts.

17The time of the annaprashana2 came;
they brought an astrologer and fixed the day firmly.

18At an auspicious moment they put prasada into the son's mouth,
and both rejoiced, clasping their son to their breasts.

19The time of the chudakarana3 came;
performing the rites according to rule, they gave him the sacred thread.

20A crimson cloth gleams upon his body;
seeing him, his father and mother rejoice at heart.

21On the third day the Thakura grew restless:
his lessons had stopped — he stayed at home and began to weep.4

22At this time the pandit Vidyanidhi came by;5
hearing of the break in the lessons, he was greatly pleased:

23"The boy has such a longing for learning —
it seems Srinivasa will become an expert in the sciences."

24One night Srinivasa saw in a dream:
"Study quickly, Srinivasa — you will go to Vrindavana.

25Gauda is very dear to Chaitanya;
through you he will make books of the pastimes arise here.

26Why have you stopped studying for three days?
At your parents' word I will teach you.

27But if you act against this word,
what you have learned will not come back to your mind."6

28He constantly uttered the name of Radha and Krishna with his tongue,
and so his learning went — he did not go to study.

29Lakshmipriya and the Acharya were astonished:
they could not understand what kind of birth this was.7

30He constantly uttered the name of Radha and Krishna with his tongue,
and so his learning went — yet there was joy in his heart.

31Sitting at home, what does Srinivasa say?
"I have not become a pandit" — such is the pain in his mind.

32"I cannot understand Krishna's mercy;
scholarship comes from study — such is its way.8

33Therefore I will not live in Yajigrama:
for the sake of learning I will go to another land."

34After ten days his mother bade him:
"Go and study, my son; your lessons have been interrupted."

35"As you command," he said, and taking a book in his hand,
Srinivasa went to his guru's place.

36Dhananjaya Vidyanivasa said a wondrous thing:
"Looking at your form, I feel joy.

37Listen, listen, Srinivasa, I will tell you:
learning no longer comes alive in me — why have you come?

38You have stolen all my learning;
I am an empty body, I tell you.

39I cannot understand your nature;
it seems Sarasvati has turned against me."

40Ashamed, Srinivasa bowed to his guru,
and Dhananjaya started up in fear, crying "Alas, alas!"

41Srinivasa's shame grew all the more, doubling;
dejected, he tied up his book and went away.

42His father and mother knew nothing of all this;
grieving over the break in his studies, he lay down alone.

43The meal was ready, but the boy was not at home;
his father went to look for him with an anxious heart.

44The pandit said: "He left a long time ago."
Finding no trace of him, the father was greatly distressed.

45Going into the house, he entered the room
and saw him asleep with a book in his hand.

46Hearing his father's voice, out of shame he said nothing,
and saying "Give me food, Mother," began to laugh.

47Having eaten, Srinivasa rinsed his mouth
and, laughing, lay down again.

48Suddenly a voice from heaven was heard in the room —
the sound came: "All learning shall awaken in you!

49I am Sarasvati; by Chaitanya's command
I have come in the guise of a dream to give you learning."

50Opening his eyes, he looks — there is no one in the room.
"By the goddess's boon I shall have great learning!"

51Laughing, he came out happily
and stood before his father and mother.

52"Come, come, my son, let me take you on my lap;
do not grieve over the break in your studies," and she kissed his cheek.9

53From then on there was no further break in his studies,
and beyond that, the name of Radha and Krishna awoke in him.

54He whose hope is the feet of Sri Jahnava and Virachandra,
Nityananda Dasa, tells the Prema-vilasa.

Thus ends the third vilasa, containing the description of the interruption of Srinivasa Acharya Thakura's studies.

Notes

  1. Variant: "Do not hold the irregularities of my writing against me."
  2. Annaprashana, a child's first feeding with rice.
  3. Chudakarana, the rite of the first tonsure; the sacred thread is normally given at the upanayana, but the text runs the two rites together.
  4. After the upanayana a boy customarily spends some days in seclusion and does not go to his teacher.
  5. Variant: "Sri Rama Vachaspati came by".
  6. Variant: "you will forget what you have learned". Who speaks in the dream is not stated; from the context, apparently the teacher.
  7. In the 1913 edition this couplet is in brackets.
  8. The second line is unclear; literally "having studied, his scholarship in such conduct".
  9. In the 1913 edition this couplet is in brackets.
